title: Tennessee halts executions after Christa Pike survives two lethal injection attempts
description: Executions in Tennessee have been halted for the rest of the year, Governor Bill Lee has said, after two attempts to execute death row inmate Christa
body: Executions in Tennessee have been halted for the rest of the year, Governor Bill Lee has said, after two attempts to execute death row inmate Christa Pike by lethal injection failed.Speaking to reporters on Thursday, Lee said he was "highly disappointed" about the botched execution, which he called one of the state's "most serious responsibilities". He has ordered an independent review.Tennessee prison officials on Wednesday attempted to administer two lethal doses of pentobarbital to Pike but she survived and was taken to hospital. Her medical condition is unclear. Pike, 50, was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of Colleen Slemmer.She was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer.Pike would have been the first woman to be executed in Tennessee for over 200 years. Lee said on Thursday the investigation into Pike's botched execution "will be thorough", adding that "it's going to take time"."There are a lot of questions," Lee said. "The people of our state deserve to have those questions answered, and that's what this investigation is for." Lee has not made clear who will conduct the independent review of the state's execution procedures. His order to pause all executions will overlap with the planned 3 December execution of convicted murderer Gary Sutton.In court filings, Pike's lawyers said she needed "life-saving measures" after her botched execution. The Tennessee Department of Correction, which handled the execution, issued a statement defending its handling of the case. It said in a statement that it "followed every step of the State's lawful, established execution protocol approved by the attorney general's office"."The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective, and the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out this evening."Pike was given two doses of the chemical pentobarbital, as per state protocol when the first attempt fails, but was still alive afterwards, according to court filings."This execution is causing Ms Pike unnecessary agony and occurring in violation of his right to be executed free of cruel and unusual punishment," her lawyers said.The Tennessee attorney general's office said in a statement that it agreed with the decision to call for an investigation, adding: "We need to know what happened."Pike's attempted execution proceeded after multiple last-minute legal challenges by her lawyers had failed, overturned in the final hour by the US Supreme Court.Slemmer's mother May Martinez, who was among those who wanted the execution to take place and who travelled to Tennessee to witness it, told NBC News after the botched attempt that "it was a mess".US Republican Senator Marsha Blackburn, who is running for Tennessee governor, described the situation as "tragic"."While there should be a thorough review of what happened and why the process failed, the answer is simple: bring back the electric chair," Blackburn said.Democrat Jerri Green, Blackburn's opponent, criticised her for wanting to "bring back one of the most cruel forms of capital punishment". "As governor, I would put a moratorium on all future executions," Green said on X.This is the second time in 2026 Tennessee officials attempted and failed to execute a prisoner. In May, the execution of Tony Carruthers was called off after staff were unable to find a vein to administer a lethal drug. Carruthers was given a one-year reprieve.With additional reporting by Stephanie Hegarty, World Service correspondent

schema.headline: Tennessee halts executions after Christa Pike survives two lethal injection attempts

title: Fires break out at French schools as students protest nationwide
description: Fires have broken out at several schools in France, as students protest by blockading education institutions nationwide over school funding and studyi
body: Fires have broken out at several schools in France, as students protest by blockading education institutions nationwide over school funding and studying conditions.Blazes were reported at two high schools in Nantes, western France, while another was filmed engulfing the entrance to another in the northern city of Rouen.Students are protesting about a lack of teachers and staff, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings. University students joined the demonstrations on Thursday, citing similar demands.Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu held a crisis meeting on Thursday to discuss the unrest. The government said afterwards that the student-led demonstrations had descended into "urban violence".Both fires in Nantes spread after a bin was set alight. The blaze at the Nelson Mandela high school, in the city centre, then spread to the front of the building, damaging the entrance hall.In the southern city of Marseille, staff at Victor Hugo high school were splashed with petrol as protesters reportedly filled containers.While in the north, a headteacher at Degrugillier high school, in the village of Auchel, was injured in the ear by a wayward firework.The blockades and protests at French lycées - for 15-18 year olds and equivalent to sixth forms in the UK or high schools in the US - began last week before spreading to hundreds of schools across the country.French media report 625 people were arrested on Wednesday alone while 83 police officers were injured. More than 600 arrests had been made by midday on Thursday,  excluding Paris, broadcaster ICI reports. At least 30 universities have also reportedly been blockaded, including campuses in Rennes and Paris.On Thursday, public transport services in Marseille and Strasbourg were halted due vandalism, threats of violence and to hinder protesters from moving around.Seventeen-year-old Raphael took part in protests outside a school in Strasbourg, where barriers were used to obstruct nearby tram tracks. He voiced his frustration at his school's facilities in an interview with news agency AFP, saying some rooms had leaks and that there were not enough toilets."The building is falling apart, the cafeteria is too small. There's zero budget, zero resources, not enough supervisors," Raphael said.While France's next general election is still months away, the protests and how French authorities are responding to them has been heavily politicised.The government and hard-right politicians have blamed the hard left for igniting protests, which are being organised by a union representing lycée students.Bally Bagayoko, the mayor of a Parisian suburb and member of the radical left La France Insoumise (LFI) party defended earlier remarks in which he said violence could be legitimate in some cases - referencing cases in which protesters had allegedly been shot at while not wearing helmets or bulletproof vests.LFI leader and presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, meanwhile, stressed he was in favour of non-violent protests, while arguing that blaming the left would not solve the issues motivating the demonstrations.Earlier, leader of the hard-right National Rally Marine Le Pen said: "This is no longer about high school student protests. It is about riots organized by professionals and overseen by deputies from La France Insoumise."The presidential candidate called for a new anti-rioting law to be passed.Left-wing mayor of Marseille Benoît Payan condemned the "unacceptable violence" in his city. While young people were "legitimately concerned" about their future and public services, they must express themselves in a calm fashion, he said.Eric Ciotti, the Republicans mayor of Nice, said the parents of those found to have damaged school property should be made to pay for the repairs.

schema.headline: Fires break out at French schools as students protest nationwide

title: Trump's AI rebrand causes 'unprecedented' demand for Slovenian website names
description: Donald Trump's push to rename AI may be behind an "unprecedented" rise in registrations for domain names in Slovenia, according to its official nation
body: Donald Trump's push to rename AI may be behind an "unprecedented" rise in registrations for domain names in Slovenia, according to its official national registry.The US president wants AI to be called "super intelligence" - or SI - the same initials used by Slovenian websites.Register.si spokeswoman Klara Herman said 44,000 web addresses with the .si suffix had been registered in September, compared to less than 2,000 in August - an increase of more than 2,100%.She said the scale of activity in late September was "unprecedented" compared to the previous 12 months.Trump called for the technology to be renamed during his speech to the United Nations General Assembly in New York on 11 September."The use of the word artificial makes it sound fake," he said. "It's not fake, it's actually amazing. But we have to be careful... welcome to the new world of super intelligence."Internet domains are the unique human-readable addresses people type into their web browsers to access websites - like bbc.co.uk.Herman said registrations for .si web addresses in September stood out "very clearly" against the other months in the year, although she was "cautious" about attributing the entire increase to just Trump's comments.She said on 30 September alone, 11,000 new registrations were recorded.One possible explanation for the purchases is a practice in which people speculatively register specific domain names in case they increase in value later on and can be sold for a profit.For example, in 1997 Rick Schwartz, known as "The Domain King", bought the domain name men.com for $15,000 (£11,300). He sold it for $1.32 million seven years later.Trump hosted a meeting of top technology bosses for what he called "an extraordinary gathering" of the people "building America's Golden Age" on Tuesday.He signed an executive order instructing US government departments and agencies to start using the terms "SI" and "Super Intelligence", and to no longer acknowledge the use of the term AI.SI will take the place of AI in "official correspondence", websites, reports and other forms of communication, the order said.Images of the signatures for the order were mocked online, external however - when it was discovered "United States" had been spelt incorrectly underneath Trump's signature.Correction 1 October:  An earlier version of this article referred to cyber-squatting, whereby people register domain names in bad faith with the intent to profit. We cited as an example the registration of men.com by Rick Schwartz. The article was amended to delete the reference to cyber-squatting and make clear simply registering domain names as an investment in the hope they will increase in value, as happened with men.com, is a legitimate business activity.

schema.headline: Trump's AI rebrand causes 'unprecedented' demand for Slovenian website names

title: Naomi Campbell wins appeal over charity ban
description: Model Naomi Campbell has won her appeal against a ban on being a charity trustee, after a tribunal ruled that she was unaware of misconduct at her cha
body: Model Naomi Campbell has won her appeal against a ban on being a charity trustee, after a tribunal ruled that she was unaware of misconduct at her charity Fashion for Relief.Campbell was banned from being a charity trustee for five years in 2024 after a watchdog found that Fashion for Relief funds had been spent on luxury hotels and spa treatments.However, a tribunal said on Thursday, external that the most serious instances of misconduct in the charity "were concealed" from Campbell by a fellow trustee."Ms Campbell was not involved in, and did not know of, that conduct," the three-person tribunal panel said.The supermodel set up Fashion for Relief to help victims of Hurricane Katrina in 2005, and went on to front further campaigns for disasters and causes around the world.However, the charity was shut in 2023 and Campbell and two other trustees were banned the following year after a Charity Commission inquiry found "serious mismanagement and/or misconduct" at Fashion for Relief, which was not passing on as much of the money raised as it was supposed to.Campbell appealed, saying one of her fellow trustees, lawyer Bianka Hellmich, forged her signature and impersonated her using a fake email address to misdirect money that was intended for the charity.Her "only mistake" was trusting Hellmich, Campbell told the tribunal in June.Hellmich has denied the allegations.The Charity Commission opposed Campbell's challenge and said the five-year ban should be upheld.In its ruling, the First-Tier Tribunal panel said Campbell's claim that she was deceived had been corroborated by documentary evidence."For the avoidance of doubt, we accept that both Ms Campbell's evidence, as well as her conduct during the operation of the Charity, was entirely honest," they said.They said Campbell did not know €4,386 (£3,750) of hotel charges from a trip to the south of France in 2018 - including €1,298 (£1,100) for dinner room service, €1,163 (£990) for spa treatments and €112 (£95) for cigarettes - had come out of the charity's expenses."The panel is satisfied that Ms Campbell was not responsible for the inappropriate use of the charity's resources or any unjustified expenditure, nor did she contribute or facilitate it," they said.Campbell must take some responsibility for failures to maintain minutes and file accounts on time - but that was not enough to disqualify the model as a charity trustee, the tribunal said."There was serious misconduct and mismanagement in the administration of the charity she founded, Fashion for Relief," the ruling said."The Tribunal has found, however, that its most serious features, including unauthorised payments to Ms Campbell's co-trustee, Bianka Hellmich, failures in the management of the Charity's finances and the misuse of its funds, resulted from Ms Hellmich's conduct and were concealed from Ms Campbell."Unauthorised payments of more than £290,000 were made to Hellmich for apparent consultancy fees, the inquiry found.The tribunal ruling continued: "Ms Hellmich deceived Ms Campbell, used forged documents and a false email address purporting to belong to her, and also deceived professional advisers and the Commission."Ms Campbell was not involved in, and did not know of, that conduct."The Tribunal finds that she had no reasonable basis to suspect Ms Hellmich's dishonesty before regulatory concerns emerged and, when they did, Ms Campbell took reasonable steps in response."Following the judgment, Campbell thanked the tribunal and the judges "for taking the time to hear my side, look at the evidence, and see the truth of what happened".The supermodel said: "Giving back has been part of who I am, so having that questioned hurt deeply."Now I can get back to what matters most to me: being there for the people and communities I've always wanted to serve."Thank you to my higher power."BBC News has tried to contact Hellmich.In April 2025, she told the Financial Times, external: "It is deeply distressing that Naomi Campbell is making these false accusations."Her claims are a device carefully designed to paint her as a victim, while scapegoating a so-called friend."This is testament to the sort of behaviour I endured during this difficult and damaging relationship. I have fully co-operated with the Charity Commission over the past six years."I am grateful this challenging period of my life is over. I hope that Naomi finds peace and happiness in her future."On Thursday, a Charity Commission spokesperson said: "We made the disqualification order for Ms Campbell based on the evidence available to us at the time."The court recognised that Ms Campbell, the Commission and the law firm concerned were subject to sophisticated deception by one of the other trustees. This was referred to the Metropolitan Police when we became aware."We acknowledge and will reflect on the court's decision and are considering any wider implications for our work."The Charity Commission also said its intervention ensured other charities including Save the Children received almost £250,000 that was owed to them.

schema.headline: Naomi Campbell wins appeal over charity ban

title: Flight attacker 'underwent Islamist radical indoctrination', Netanyahu says
description: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesByOlivia IrelandIsraeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says investigations suggest the man who stabbed his fellow
body: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesByOlivia IrelandIsraeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says investigations suggest the man who stabbed his fellow pilot and tried to take over a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv had undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination".The Flydubai plane plunged more than 17,000ft (5,200m) two hours into its journey on Wednesday, before passengers and crew overpowered the attacker and retook control to land safely.Speaking to Fox News, Netanyahu also said it was looking "very likely" that the attacker, who he said was an Omani national, "was going to down the plane".Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) state news agency reports investigations have begun there to determine "whether the incident was linked to any terrorist activity or purpose".Figure caption, Passenger Almog Itali said it felt like a "rollercoaster" as Flight FZ1073 fell 17,000ft in less than two minutesThe co-pilot is currently being questioned in Saudi Arabia, where the plane made an emergency landing. However UAE officials say they have jurisdiction over the incident because the aircraft on which the attack took place is registered there and flies under its flag.Netanyahu told Fox that once the attacker had been subdued and tied up by passengers and crew, he was "calling out to the aircrew 'kill me, kill me', so it's clear he was suicidal that's not a question"."And with all the passengers in there, and if you couple that with what I just told you about the Islamist tendencies, that radicalisation that were found in his background, I think ... that'll give us a pretty good clue but again I don't make final conclusions yet but that's the indications we have now." The prime minister was also asked earlier on the same network whether there was an indication if Iran was involved, he replied: "It's too early to say".The attacker was arrested in Saudi Arabia and is expected to be transferred to the UAE, Netanyahu said.Both Netanyahu and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said the stabbed pilot, Indian national Capt Smit Machchhar was a "hero". India's ambassador to the UAE Deepak Mittal visited Captain Machhar in hospital on Thursday, the Indian Mission confirmed on social media, stating he was "in good health and recovering well". Image source, Embassy of India in IsraelImage caption, The Indian government has praised Smit Machchhar for his "immense courage"Preliminary findings from a separate Israeli investigation into the incident, suggest that the alleged attacker intended to crash the plane, an Israeli security source told BBC Arabic.The source said the investigation - led by Israel's intelligence agency Mossad - interviewed passengers after they arrived in Tel Aviv to establish what had happened on the plane.Flydubai's flight FZ1073, with more than 170 people on board, took off from Dubai International Airport in the UAE at 03:05 GMT (07:05 local time), en route to Ben Gurion Airport.Two hours later, the 17,000ft drop in altitude was reported on the plane tracking website Flightradar24 and minutes later the plane signalled an emergency code.At about 05:40, the plane - which had briefly entered Jordanian airspace - looped back into Saudi Arabia, where it later started its manual descent, landing safely at  Tabuk Airport in the north west of Saudi.Flydubai has since suspended flights between Dubai and Tel Aviv as it carried out its own investigation into the incident.Israel's Transportation Ministry said the suspension aligns with Netanyahu's directive.Israeli airlines including El Al, Israir and Arkia said plans were in place to operate rescue flights from Dubai starting on Friday to bring back stranded passengers. The Transportation Ministry also said it sent an urgent request to Etihad Airlines to increase the number of flights between Abu Dhabi and Tel Aviv.

schema.headline: Flight attacker 'underwent Islamist radical indoctrination', Netanyahu says

title: Russia targets busy Pivdennyi bridge in central Kyiv
description: Two Russian drones have hit one of Kyiv's main bridges, bringing public transport in the Ukrainian capital to a halt and signalling a new stage in Mos
body: Two Russian drones have hit one of Kyiv's main bridges, bringing public transport in the Ukrainian capital to a halt and signalling a new stage in Moscow's attacks.The Pivdennyi or Southern bridge came under fire as a metro train was travelling across. Passengers described how dust from a blast wave entered their carriage through the ventilation system.The Pivdennyi bridge is one of the main arteries across the Dnipro river dividing western and eastern Kyiv.Kyiv's bridges had not been hit before Thursday's strikes - and despite a dramatic explosion close to a main support section, city authorities said preliminary checks "did not find any critical damage to the structure".For the people of Kyiv, the drone strikes were another powerful reminder that Russia has their city firmly in its sights and is doing everything it can to disrupt life in the capital.Kyiv had just suffered its first co-ordinated attacks on the city's energy grid since the end of last winter, and commentators believe Russia has stepped up its campaign seeing that Ukraine is suffering from a shortage of air defences.Strikes on Wednesday also heralded a return to power cuts in the capital. Although Kyiv authorities have spent months constructing smaller-scale power plants to counter Russia's anticipated winter campaign, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said a combined strike on such a scale had not taken place since the end of spring.Later in the morning, two drones hit the Pivdenny bridge, one hitting the base of a central stanchion.Ukrainian 5 Kanal TV reporter Mariana Mykytenko described how one of the passengers on her metro train shouted the word "Shahed", referring to Russia's Iranian-designed drones, before the blast sent dust pouring into their carriage.No-one in her compartment was hurt, she said, and "the train took people to Vydubychi station on the right bank, then it didn't go any further". The right bank is on the west side of the Dnipro river.Metro trains were suspended but road traffic was eventually allowed to resume. It is not yet clear what kind of drone was used in the Kyiv bridge attack, but Ukrainian officials say a new design of Russia's jet-powered drones came into operation for the first time on Wednesday.The drone has a 40kg warhead and is especially designed to destroy high-voltage electricity pylons and iron bridge structures, according to Zelensky's technology adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov, also known as Flash.In recent weeks, Russia has had considerable success with jet-powered drones and Ukrainian air force officials say that, during September, at least 3,177 were launched. Their high speed has caused problems for Ukraine's beleaguered air defences.Kyiv's Institute of Nuclear Research came under drone attack on Wednesday night and, earlier in the week, one person was killed when a drone targeted the National Academy of Sciences.

schema.headline: Russia targets busy Pivdennyi bridge in central Kyiv

title: Lib Dems criticise Ed Davey over pension triple lock response
description: Liberal Democrat MPs have criticised their party leader over his defence of the pension triple lock. Senior Lib Dems, who are on the party's frontbenc
body: Liberal Democrat MPs have criticised their party leader over his defence of the pension triple lock. Senior Lib Dems, who are on the party's frontbench, have privately attacked Sir Ed Davey for his response to the prime minister's plans to adjust the policy, which guarantees the state pension goes up each year in line with either inflation, wage increases, or 2.5% – whichever is highest.They joined unsolicited criticism in public and private from others in the party, with one saying the majority of Lib Dem MPs disagree with their leader.It comes after Sir Ed told the BBC removing the triple lock "would put more pensioners into poverty"."This would mean people who are working hard now - the millennials - when they retire would have a very poor pension," he told the Today programme.Under Andy Burnham's plan - which he hopes will raise £15bn a year by the end of the 2030s - the automatic annual link with average earnings would be removed from 2030 so the state pension rises with at least 2.5% or inflation, whichever is higher."His proposals are to deal with social care in the next decade when it needs to be done now," Sir Ed said."It's a little bit of a vibe. It's not a solution," he said.But multiple Lib Dems at different levels have now criticised Sir Ed's response.A Lib Dem MP contacted the BBC after Sir Ed's interview to say the majority of the parliamentary party would not support opposing Burnham's changes to the triple lock.Another, Tom Gordon, who represents Harrogate & Knaresborough, said Sir Ed's criticism of Burnham's plan to adjust the triple lock was "nonsense" and "gaslights an entire generation into believing it's for our benefit".He wrote on X: "The idea that we're keeping the triple lock to help millennials is at best for the birds, and at worst downright insulting. I say that as a millennial."He added: "Telling millennials we're keeping the triple lock to help us in 30 years' time is nonsense."We're on course to be the first generation worse off than our parents. We're locked out of the housing market, paying higher taxes, repaying student loans that never seem to shrink, and putting off having children because of the cost of living."Vikki Slade, the party's MP for Mid-Dorset and North Poole, said on Bluesky: "Most millennials don't think there will be a state pension when they retire so this isn't being done with them in mind."She added that she was "proud" of the triple lock when it was introduced by the Conservative-Liberal Democrat coalition government in 2010, "but we must plan for future not venerate the past".A Lib Dem spokesperson said: "The triple lock has always been controversial. "It's done a lot of good but its job isn't done yet, so Labour's plan would push too many of today's workers into poverty when they retire."We want Andy Burnham to get back around the table so that we can find a lasting consensus on social care with a sustainable funding model - not one pulled out of the pockets of a group of people who can least afford it."The Lib Dems, and other opposition parties, are battling to respond to a new set of priorities from the Labour government under Burnham. One frontbench Lib Dem MP told the BBC after Burnham's Labour conference speech: "Lots of us [are] struggling tonight with [a] Labour leader articulating Lib Dem values better than we do."They pointed to Burnham's promises on electoral reform, social care, the water industry, and relations with Europe - all Lib Dem campaign points in recent years."I'm honestly utterly despondent with the state of things," another Lib Dem MP said.Some senior Lib Dems believe Sir Ed's position as leader has been vulnerable for some time, even if they stressed no challenge is imminent."A plausible candidate could take him tomorrow in a bloodless coup," one prominent party figure said. "But that person hasn't yet revealed themselves as far as I'm aware. Nobody is going to blow anything up without a clear plan to put something in its place."

schema.headline: Lib Dems criticise Ed Davey over pension triple lock response

title: Man City: HMRC urged to scrutinise tax implications of verdict revealed by Premier League
description: Manchester City, who deny wrongdoing, will claim as part of their appeal that key sponsorship deals were funded by the Abu Dhabi government, rather th
body: Manchester City, who deny wrongdoing, will claim as part of their appeal that key sponsorship deals were funded by the Abu Dhabi government, rather than the club's owners.Owners Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG) - a private investment company belonging to United Arab Emirates vice-president and deputy prime minister Sheikh Mansour - are said to have topped up the value of commercial deals as part of a "disguised funding scheme" to the scale of £830.69m.This, it was argued, enabled the club to appear to comply with Premier League and Uefa financial rules.However, as first reported by the Daily Mail and Times, sources have told BBC Sport that City are expected to tell an appeal board that they have evidence showing the money directed to sponsors came from the Abu Dhabi government, rather than from ADUG.The independent commission rejected this argument as "untrue" in its findings, saying: "We concluded that it was an 'explanation' that the club had concocted well after the event in an attempt to obscure and conceal the realities of the disguised funding scheme."City have claimed the commission's decision contained "clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe".Mansour is a member of the ruling family of Abu Dhabi, and the brother of UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan. ADUG took over City in 2008. Premier League rules allow state-owned bodies to sponsor clubs.On Saturday, City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak referred to "irrefutable evidence" that he claimed supports the club's claims of innocence.City's principal sponsor Etihad Airways has said it is considering legal action against the Premier League, claiming the release of the commission findings had "damaging implications… despite the airline not being named in the redacted published findings".The UAE's state-owned national airline said it "categorically rejects any finding, conclusion or implication that suggests the airline has ever been involved in improper commercial arrangements".Etihad is owned by sovereign wealth fund L'Imad which is chaired by the Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, the son of the UAE president.The Premier League declined to comment when contacted by BBC Sport.

schema.headline: Man City: HMRC urged to scrutinise tax implications of verdict revealed by Premier League

title: Captain Smit Machchhar: The 'hero' India pilot who was stabbed on Israel-bound flight
description: Machchhar grew up in the Indian city of Mumbai, where his parents still live. In 2008, he joined Mainland Air, an aviation college in New Zealand's Du
body: Machchhar grew up in the Indian city of Mumbai, where his parents still live. In 2008, he joined Mainland Air, an aviation college in New Zealand's Dunedin, before joining Indian airline SpiceJet as a commercial pilot three years later. He moved to Dubai and joined Flydubai in 2022 as an experienced pilot.Philip Kean, the CEO of Mainland Air, told the BBC he remembered Machchhar as a man who would remain calm in a crisis. "We trained him for forced landing - not this kind of situation, which is very, very rare," Kean said. "It was a long time back but he came across as a good and honest worker."Machchhar has more than 9,750 hours of flying experience, including more than 6,400 hours as pilot-in-command, according to his LinkedIn profile.His former employer SpiceJet issued a statement calling Machchhar a "hero" who had saved "countless lives".An old friend who worked with him at SpiceJet, Capt Dharav Gosalia, described him as outgoing and "very jovial".Machchhar - whose nickname was "Smit Mac" - was a "disciplined flier" who had undergone years of training, he said, including from former Indian Air Force pilots who had moved into commercial aviation.Last year, Machchhar spoke about how he started flying and his experiences as a pilot on a podcast called Bona-Fide Banter.Aviation, he said, was "never a childhood dream". When he was around 19, he joined a management course, planning to work for his family's business. But then he came across an aviation seminar and "the bug bit [him]", he added.Machchhar also spoke about how, when he wore his pilot's uniform, he was "no-nonsense" and thought "about work 100%". But unlike his younger days, he added, he now placed a greater value on having a healthy work-life balance and spending time with family."Give personal life equal importance - it will help you fly longer," he advised.He also detailed challenges he had faced in the air, including when a passenger went into early labour and the crew worked together to ensure the baby was born safely."In aviation terms, I was lucky to grow up with people who helped me be the pilot that I am today," he said, crediting senior pilots with teaching him how to face stressful situations.At the time of the conversation, Machchhar said that no plane he'd flown had needed to make an emergency landing. He had, however, faced medical emergencies and minor aircraft issues that had caused delays.He said delays were "not my problem. As long as you're walking out of the aircraft [safely], that's what I want."Indian social media has been awash with praise for Machchhar since his identity emerged, with commenters calling him a hero. Snippets from the podcast have also gone viral.Flydubai's flight FZ1073 took off from Dubai International Airport in the United Arab Emirates at 03:05 GMT (07:05 local time) en route to Ben Gurion Airport in Israel.The flight was carrying at least 150 people, with Netanyahu saying "almost all" passengers were Israeli.Data from flight tracking website Flightradar24 shows the plane made a rapid descent over Saudi Arabia around two and a half hours after take-off, dropping more than 17,000ft (5,000m) in less than two minutes at around 05:21.Minutes later, the plane signalled an emergency code - squawk 7700 - before switching it to a squawk 7500 code, which indicates a hijacking.At 05:40, the plane - which had briefly entered Jordanian airspace - looped back into Saudi Arabia, where it later started its manual descent for landing.Less than an hour later, the plane returned to squawk 7700.Initial local media reports cited Israeli officials as saying a fight had broken out between two pilots.But speaking on Wednesday after the incident, Netanyahu confirmed later reports that one pilot had stabbed the other before "apparently trying to crash" the plane.He said an Israeli passenger told him "the plane went into a spin and began to descend" before the passenger and a crew member broke into the cockpit and overpowered the "pilot who had carried out the stabbing".The plane was diverted to Tabuk Airport in north-western Saudi Arabia and touched down at 06:58, according to location data.The stabbed pilot, who is in a stable condition according to the Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia, was later identified as Machchhar.

schema.headline: Captain Smit Machchhar: The 'hero' India pilot who was stabbed on Israel-bound flight

title: Travelodge failed Maidenhead sex assault victim 'at every stage'
description: Greaney said blame rested with Travelodge, that has its HQ in Thame, Oxfordshire, as an organisation rather than with individual staff, and a culture
body: Greaney said blame rested with Travelodge, that has its HQ in Thame, Oxfordshire, as an organisation rather than with individual staff, and a culture had developed in which room intrusions were regarded as "one of those things".The woman emailed a complaint to Travelodge in January 2023, addressed to chief executive Jo Boydell and others.The review concluded the email was handled by her office without her knowledge, and did not come to Boydell's attention until March 2026.The woman's complaint was instead investigated by a manager who was himself criticised in it, and the customer services team offered her a refund for her night's stay, which she understood to be £30.Boydell stepped down as chief executive in August following criticism over the company's handling of safety complaints. The review said she deserved credit for driving improvements from March.The attack became national news in March after the woman contacted the BBC, saying the case raised serious questions about room security at Travelodge hotels.Since then, dozens of people have shared experiences of strangers entering their rooms, including a domestic abuse victim whose abuser was given a key to her room at a Travelodge in London.Then-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer wrote to Boydell in March urging her to "seriously engage" with the government over security. Greaney was appointed to lead the review the following month.The review makes 38 recommendations, including moving towards a system that requires guests to show ID to get a room key, which Travelodge has been trialling at some hotels since May.It also calls for body-worn cameras for reception staff, better checks that staff have understood their training, and for housekeepers to always send guests to reception.Greaney said Travelodge must "urgently" create a policy on violence against women and girls, drawn up with the Suzy Lamplugh Trust, and train all staff in it.The review said changes made this year had been done quickly "albeit years too late" and its new key security policy would prevent a repeat of the Maidenhead attack if applied correctly.But it found the policy was "not being applied with anything like sufficient consistency on the ground".Mystery shoppers were able to get into rooms through housekeeping staff at all five hotels tested, including Maidenhead, without being sent to reception or asked for proof they were entitled to enter.At three of the hotels, staff confirmed a guest was staying there, and at two, room numbers were said out loud at check-in. The Maidenhead hotel scored worst of the five.Other recommendations included networked CCTV across the chain and key card-controlled access to all residential corridors.Greaney said room intrusions were a problem across the hotel sector.He praised the woman's courage and determination, saying the problems would have remained "beneath the surface" had she not shared her experience.Freddie van Mierlo, the Liberal Democrat MP for Henley and Thame, where Travelodge is based, said he was worried the company was "still trying to do safety on the cheap".He said the review's recommendations would require "significant capital investment", and Travelodge needed to make clear it was prepared to deliver that.In response, a Travelodge spokesperson said: "We are committed to implementing the recommendations and will make the necessary investments to do so. "We cannot provide a specific figure but can assure people that all required investments in guest safety will be made and we have the resources required."Ray Reidy, Travelodge's interim chief executive, said the review made clear there were failures in its policies and in the way customers had been treated."I apologise unreservedly on behalf of Travelodge to all guests where we have failed," he said. "We have made significant progress in preventing and addressing these issues over the past six months, and we recognise we still have further to go."Travelodge said a new board committee would oversee the changes, with independent assessments of its progress after six and 12 months.

schema.headline: Travelodge failed Maidenhead sex assault victim 'at every stage'

title: Hundreds of jobs under threat at Grangemouth chemical plant
description: Image caption, Syngenta said its Grangemouth facility was "no longer competitive"ByJames DelaneyBBC ScotlandUpdated 14 minutes agoHundreds of jobs are
body: Image caption, Syngenta said its Grangemouth facility was "no longer competitive"ByJames DelaneyBBC ScotlandUpdated 14 minutes agoHundreds of jobs are under threat in Grangemouth after an agricultural chemical firm announced plans to cease operations at the site.Syngenta said it had been unable to make its business at the plant "competitive" in the face of "increasing international competition".A spokesperson for the company - which manufactures chemicals used for the protection of crops - said it would enter a consultation period over the move, but added a final decision has yet to be taken.The Economy Secretary, Stephen Flynn, described the plans as "extremely disappointing".The UK government's Reindustrialisation Minister, Blair McDougall, said they had worked with Scottish counterparts to "explore every possible avenue" for support, but Syngenta had taken the decision on a commercial basis.A total of 377 workers are set to be affected by the move.It comes over a year after Syngenta was awarded £2.2m from Scottish Enterprise to expand production at the site.Syngenta added that it was "committed to genuine consultation" with trade unions over "alternative paths" for the site.The firm said it had undertaken a "detailed review" of its Grangemouth operation prior to the plans being announced.It said the Grangemouth site was "significantly more expensive" to operate than other production facilities.The company added that savings had been identified in some areas of the business, but these fell short in "bridging the site's competitiveness gap".Mike Hollands, president of Syngenta UK, said: "The workforce at Grangemouth is highly skilled and passionate, but despite all efforts, we have not been able to make the Grangemouth site competitive compared to alternative supply options."It is with a very heavy heart that we make this proposal, but we are committed to a constructive consultation and will continue to consider options as part of that process."'Strong opposition'It is the latest job loss blow to the area following the closure of the nearby oil refinery in April last year, which also resulted in the loss of about 400 jobs.In March, bus manufacturer Alexander Dennis announced plans to close its Falkirk plant with 115 roles lost.The UK government, under then-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer, previously pledged an additional £200m in funding for Grangemouth from the National Wealth Fund.Flynn said the Scottish government had "strongly opposed" Syngenta's plans.He said he would continue to press the UK government on the £200m funding pot."My thoughts are with the workers, their families and the local community who will be affected by this decision," he said."We made clear to Syngenta's board our strong opposition to any potential scale down or closure of their Grangemouth site."Flynn added: "During this period of consultation, I sincerely hope that the UK government will now provide some of the £200m committed to Grangemouth, since not a single penny has yet been allocated from that fund promised in 2024."McDougall said the UK government would work with the National Wealth Fund in the coming days to "explore all options for the area"."I know this will be a deeply concerning time for workers at Syngenta and their families, and I met with the company earlier today to discuss all options for the site and the workforce," he said."We will continue to work closely with both of them and look at all options for the site and the workforce."'Pull out the stops to protect jobs'Scottish Conservative Central Scotland MSP Meghan Gallacher said: "This is another hammer blow for Grangemouth and my thoughts are with the workers who are set to lose their jobs."Grangemouth and the surrounding communities have been devastated by the closure of major sites in recent years and this will have a further deeply damaging impact on the local and national economy."Both SNP and Labour ministers must pull out all the stops to try and protect these jobs and offer support to those who will be affected."The Scottish Green Party co-leader, Gillian Mackay, who is also a local MSP, said the move was another "devastating blow" for the area."Our governments should be doing more to protect jobs and ensure that workers can benefit from our transition to a greener future," she said."Grangemouth is my home, and I am concerned about what this will mean for the local community if it goes ahead."

schema.headline: Hundreds of jobs under threat at Grangemouth chemical plant

title: 'Overcrowded' and 'set up to fail': Freed prisoners react to early release scheme
description: Figure caption, Watch: Freed prisoners speak to the BBC as they are released earlyByTom McArthurUpdated 1 hour agoAs hundreds of prisoners across Engl
body: Figure caption, Watch: Freed prisoners speak to the BBC as they are released earlyByTom McArthurUpdated 1 hour agoAs hundreds of prisoners across England and Wales are released early under a new scheme designed to free up prison space, some of those freed have told the BBC of the "hectic" conditions they are leaving behind - and their concerns about a lack of support waiting for them outside.Around 700 offenders are expected to be freed with the first wave on Thursday, as prisoners serving sentences of up to 19 months become eligible for release after a third of their term.The government has stressed they will remain subject to strict monitoring arrangements, including the expanded use of electronic tagging, and has said action was needed to prevent prisons from becoming full.But some victims have questioned how they will be protected, while a probation worker told the BBC that managing the influx of offenders may be "just too much".Outside Wandsworth Prison in London, former bus driver Michael Bogle was adamant he would not return to the Victorian-era facility - describing the conditions as "awful".He served 78 days for shoplifting soap detergent, and had initially been given a suspended 32-week sentence but had breached it. Bogle told reporters offenders were locked up for 23 hours a day. He said he knew of one prisoner who had recently taken his own life.The early release scheme should continue, he said: "It's good. Tagging is better than prison".Another man released from Wandsworth on Thursday - who declined to be named and said he had been sentenced for "taking things without paying for them" - said the prison was "so crowded even the rats are complaining".Some prisoners were surprised by their release. Benjamin Stewart, 46, said he was only told he was being let out of HMP Birmingham after a knock on his cell door on Thursday morning."I didn't have a clue I was getting out," he told the BBC.'It's disgusting in there'Matthew Johnson, 35 also spoke of poor conditions as he expressed relief to be leaving Leeds Prison.He said he had been released after six months from an 18 month sentence for actual bodily harm.Asked what he would say to opponents of early release, he said: "You want to see what's inside these rooms, then you'll know."It's hectic. It's crowded. It's overcrowded – cells for one person with two people in them."He added: "Staff are overwhelmed anyway with what they've got to cope with at the minute".Image caption, Jake Sykes said he expected to be fitted with an electronic tag on Thursday afternoonJake Sykes, 33, similarly spoke of "disgusting" conditions as he left Lincoln Prison, after being sentenced to 16 weeks in prison for shoplifting.He will be tagged, banned from going to the pub and have a curfew.Sykes said overcrowding inside was "bad", with prisoners sharing cells, adding: "It's full of cockroaches, rats. It's disgusting in there, filthy."But he said the justice system's biggest problem was the lack of support for offenders after they leave prison."The support is there whilst you're there, so you're secure, you feel safe there," he said."And then when you get out, there's nothing."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, David, 50, said he was convicted for stealing some glassesBack in London, a man who gave his name only as David as he left HMP Brixton said he did not believe the scheme could work, because of a lack of support for inmates on the outside.He feared the justice system was "setting us up to fail"."Stop sending people to prison in the first place. Help them before they get there," he said."I've been in and out of prison all my life. It's help I need", he added.The number of people expected to be released under this scheme was cut from around 6,000 after the prime minister intervened to review its terms, removing eligibility for crimes including all forms of manslaughter, grooming offences and causing or allowing the death of a child.Early release will not apply to indeterminate sentences, which are handed out for the most serious offences like murder, and require a parole board to deem a prisoner safe to be released.Those released early can immediately be returned to prison if they breach the terms of their licence, including by committing another crime, contacting a victim or living at an address not approved by authorities.However, London Victims' Commissioner Andrea Simon is among those to have raised concerns about the provisions in place - warning the exemptions do not include "some offenders whose imminent release is a genuinely terrifying prospect for their victims".Meanwhile, concerns have been voiced about the probation system's ability to manage those released. Earlier this week, the Chief Inspector of Probation Martin Jones said the electronic monitoring regime had "not kept pace" and could create "a false sense of assurance" unless failing are addressed.

schema.headline: 'Overcrowded' and 'set up to fail': Freed prisoners react to early release scheme

title: 'I love the sheep and the people' - Knitters flock to Shetland's wool week
description: Image caption, Shetland Wool Week draw visitors from Scotland and further afieldByJohn JohnstonBBC Scotland NewsReporting fromLerwick, ShetlandUpdated
body: Image caption, Shetland Wool Week draw visitors from Scotland and further afieldByJohn JohnstonBBC Scotland NewsReporting fromLerwick, ShetlandUpdated 1 October 2026 06:23 BSTAlmost 1,000 people have gathered in Shetland for the island's annual celebration of wool, knitting and textiles.The week-long event is marking its 17th year and features classes, workshops, talks, tours and social activities.Shetland Wool Week draws enthusiasts from around the world, including the US and Japan.This year's patron, knitwear designer Helen Robertson, said: "I think wool week is just such a fantastic organisation and festival, and it's really brought Shetland textiles to life."Nancy Woodhouse, a knitter from Arizona in the US, brought some of her creations, including a woolly hat inspired by the crime drama Shetland."I love the show," she said.Describing the head wear, Woodhouse said: "We start on the hat with detective Jimmy Perez of course and Tosh who's taken over as the lead detective, then we have the ever helpful Sandy and Ruth Calder, and this is the chalk outline of the victim. "The hat has muted colours so the detectives would shine - it's the crime scene I wear on my head."Image caption, Nancy Woodhouse is a fan of the crime drama ShetlandImage caption, The hat features characters from the showSatoko Nagakubo has flown from Tokyo for the festival."I come from Japan many times to Shetland for wool week because I love the sheep and the local people. I love Shetland lace knitting and spinning," she said.Mary Randles, visiting from Lancashire, said: "I think the fact that you can chill, you can knit, meet people, buy wool and sit on your suitcase until it forces all the wool in before you take it home."She said the event allowed her to see the sheep the wool she uses for knitting come from.Randles added: "Once you've knitted with it and washed it, it drapes beautifully whereas sometimes when you knitting with synthetic it doesn't drape but this stuff does."From Fair Isle knitting to spinning, fleece preparation, weaving, lace knitting to  wool skirting, there is a huge range for visitors to discover.It is an event that stretches far beyond the classroom, with activities taking place from Unst to the south mainland. Local communities are at the heart of the week, with community halls, crofts and businesses, makers and musicians all helping to create the unique experience for the wool enthusiasts.Patron Helen Robertson designed the much-anticipated wool week hat - the Birsie Beanny."It's such a joyful and happy week," she said.Image source, Shetland Amenity TrustImage caption, Knitwear designer Helen Robertson said the week brought Shetland's textiles to lifeImage source, Shetland Amenity TrustImage caption, Shetland Wool Week's Birsie Beanny hats were designed by Helen RobertsonThe star attraction are Shetland's native sheep and the earthy shades of cream, brown and black of their wool. Ronnie Eunson runs Uradale Farm on the west side of the islands and breeds native sheep and cattle which graze on the nearby hills and coastline.He said: "Shetland wool is a fairly unique commodity."It's the history and heritage that makes it really special. You're looking at a type of fibre that has clothed Shetlanders for thousands of years."Eunson said the sheep had a double coat of wool which protected them against the islands' harsh winter weather. The finer wool is below the top layer.The farmer added: "Tourists are fascinated to see the sheep and to hear about the way we look after the sheep and how the sheep look after themselves."Image source, SHETLAND AMENITY TRUSTImage caption, The wool is produced by sheep that are native to ShetlandAs the nights draw in and winter approaches the festival is a big boost too for the island's economy.  Donna Smith, who runs Langsoond Yarn in Burra, said: "It's really an amazing event that's the highlight of the year for me at the end of the tourist season."There are so many people coming to visit and so many people coming to buy yarn. It's such an important week in the whole year for the business.The "sewing of the loose ends" of the festival is on Saturday. Then it will be time for the hundreds of visitors to cast off and head home with their Shetland Oo for another year.

schema.headline: 'I love the sheep and the people' - Knitters flock to Shetland's wool week

title: Train speeded up past red signal before fatal Bedford rail crash
description: Image source, PA MediaImage caption, The collision happened after one train stopped and a second train passed a red signal and struck it from behindBy
body: Image source, PA MediaImage caption, The collision happened after one train stopped and a second train passed a red signal and struck it from behindByDanny FullbrookBedfordshire, Hertfordshire and BuckinghamshireA train involved in a fatal crash had accelerated past a red signal that was rarely ever on, investigators have found.Train driver Shaun Burton, 60, died and more than 160 people were injured when his London-bound service crashed into the back of another train on 19 June at Elstow, near Bedford.The Rail Accident Investigation Branch, external (RAIB) has found the signal had not displayed a red light to any train before the crash during 2026.The latest interim report said CCTV had shown the signal had displayed red correctly, and Burton had acknowledged it, but he had continued to accelerate and applied brakes only seconds before hitting the other train, which had earlier come to a stop.Image source, Alex KnightImage caption, There had been 92 passengers on the Nottingham train and 155 on the Corby trainThe collision took place between two East Midlands Railway (EMR) services on Network Rail's Midland Main Line, about 2.5 miles (4km) south of Bedford station.The driver of the first train, travelling from Nottingham to London, was learning how to operate a new type of train under the supervision of an instructor.It stopped after receiving an Automatic Warning System (AWS) alert, despite the signal ahead displaying green.Neither the driver nor the instructor recognised the alarm as an AWS warning, and it was not acknowledged within the required window. This caused the train's emergency brakes to be applied automatically.When Burton's train approached from Corby, the signal was displaying red, although he acknowledged its AWS warning, he continued to accelerate.RAIB said no train had previously been recorded passing the signal while it was red since records began in 1985.Image source, British Transport PoliceImage caption, Train driver Shaun Burton, from Cambridgeshire, died in the train crash near BedfordOn 9 July, after the crash, another train approaching the same signal received an incorrect AWS warning despite it displaying green.The AWS equipment was later found to be positioned 16mm below rail level, outside the permitted tolerance. Investigators are examining whether this contributed to the incorrect warnings.However, investigators found no evidence that the signal itself was faulty when it was tested after the crash.RAIB said it would continue to investigate why Burton's train had passed the red signal, as well as the signal's positioning, visibility and status.Do you have a story suggestion for Beds, Herts or Bucks? Contact us below.Get in touchYour Voice

schema.headline: Train speeded up past red signal before fatal Bedford rail crash
